claims.text: Controlled post-processing annealing of HfZrTiTa0.53 can improve tensile ductility.
Controlled post-processing annealing can increase the uniform elongation of HfZrTiTa0.53.
Annealing improves ductility by modifying the alloy's grain-boundary structure.
Annealing improves ductility by relieving internal stress.
The proposed annealing treatment will preserve the alloy's high yield strength.
The proposed annealing treatment will preserve impact-triggered chemical-energy release.
The as-processed HfZrTiTa0.53 baseline has a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
The as-processed HfZrTiTa0.53 baseline has a compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
The as-processed HfZrTiTa0.53 baseline has a terminal strain of 13.5%.
Limited tensile ductility was observed in the reported as-processed HfZrTiTa0.53 state.
Annealing below full recrystallization can provide partial stress relief in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Annealing below full recrystallization can stabilize the grain boundaries of HfZrTiTa0.53.
The treatment will produce a refined microstructure with more uniform and stabilized grain boundaries.
The treatment will reduce internal stress concentrations.
Residual-stress relief and a more uniform grain-boundary structure enhance dislocation mobility.
Residual-stress relief and grain-boundary uniformity suppress localized strain concentration.
At room temperature and the baseline strain rate, annealed specimens will have uniform elongation exceeding 13.5%.
The prediction is limited to room-temperature tensile loading at the unspecified baseline strain rate.
Matched compression and impact tests should be conducted alongside tensile tests.
Failure to increase uniform elongation above 13.5%, or a significant loss of yield strength or impact-energy release, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% baseline is identified as terminal strain, but it is subsequently used as though it were the baseline tensile uniform elongation. Terminal strain and tensile uniform elongation are distinct measurements, so exceeding 13.5% uniform elongation is not a valid relative comparison without establishing that the reported 13.5% came from the same tensile metric.
